note.title: Volodimerko Volodarič
note.p: Volodimerko Volodarič was another in the line of rulers of Volodymyr–Volyn′ and Halyč, following in the footsteps of his father and uncle Volodar′ and Vasil′ko. The question here is who Volodimerko’s wife was and thus who was the mother of Jaroslav Osmomysl, one of the most famous members of this line of rulers? The Rusian chronicles contain no mention of such a woman, though Tatiščev’s work does. Tatiščev records a fascinating encounter, one that is recorded no where else that I have seen, under the year 1126, in which Volodimerko and his brother Rostislav went to war for control of their father’s territory. Tatiščev, Istorija Rossiiskaja, vol. 2, 138. The battle is important because during it, as during many battles we have seen, the two sides expanded the conflict seeking aid. /Rostislav Volodarič called on his cousins the Vasilkoviči for assistance, while Volodimerko sent to the Hungarians. Moreover, when things turned against Volodimerko, he took his wife and children and fled to his “test′” in Hungary. Ibid. Ruling at the time in Hungary was Stephen II, the son of Koloman. Stephen II had just married in 1121, and so it is impossible that he had a daughter who would have already been married to Volodimerko and produced children. For Stephen’s marriage, see Wertner, Az Árpádok családi története, chart. In this instance “test′” is used beyond its modern meaning of “father–in–law” to mean “brother–in–law.” Numerous examples of this are present in all of the Rusian chronicles. Though no daughters of Koloman are recorded by Wertner in his history of the Árpáds and their genealogy, this seems the most likely solution. Wertner, Az Árpádok családi története, chart. Further it seems unlikely that Tatiščev would make such information up out of whole cloth without providing more information. Instead of a full account of their marriage, which he has provided for others, he merely mentions her in passing as she is gathered up with the children to flee to Hungary. More so, the whole account of the strife over the territory of Volodar′ Rostislavič has the ring of truth, and the Hungarian component is only an element of the whole story, a place for Volodimerko to call for aid, find refuge, and get troops—the obvious purpose of the marriage for a western Rusian ruler. Potentially providing some measure of corroboration is an account from the Hypatian chronicle from 1144, in which Volodimerko is captured and made to swear to Vsevolod but is helped by Hungarians. Hypatian Chronicle, s.a. 1144. Though it is thin, perhaps this is a continuance of Volodimerko’s reliance on Hungarian troops because of his marriage, even though the regime had changed in Hungary.

All of this leads me to the conclusion that despite the dubious nature of the sole source, there does seem to have been a marriage between Volodimerko and a Hungarian princess and a daughter of Koloman seems a likely candidate to fit the available facts.
